# True or false: Project management

Fixed dates, fixed prices, RAID logs, stage gates and status reports. Test the habits that keep a project green on paper and red underneath.

10 statements (Foundation 4, Standard 5, Assured 1). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area project-management`.

### 1. Software that will be changed for years after launch should be funded as a project that closes at go-live.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Project funding ends at launch and leaves the service without owners, so it starts to decay. Fund a persistent product team for anything that will change for more than a year. Wrap a project around it only for a fixed end, a contract or a legal date.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/projects-and-products.md](../../playbook/project-management/projects-and-products.md)

</details>

### 2. When a contract fixes scope, date and cost all at once, quality and risk become the hidden variable.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** You can fix at most two of the three. When all three are fixed, testing gets cut and defects ship. Say so in writing before signing, and protect the go/no-go criteria, because they are the last place quality is defended.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md](../../playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md)

</details>

### 3. Estimating from how similar past projects actually turned out gives a better forecast than building the estimate from the current plan alone.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** People forecast from the plan in front of them and ignore how similar work went, which Kahneman and Tversky called the planning fallacy. Reference class forecasting starts from the real outcomes of past projects and adjusts the plan's own estimate by them.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md](../../playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md)

</details>

### 4. Contingency should be spread across work packages so that each team holds its own buffer.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Work expands to fill the time available, so buffers spread across tasks get spent whether the risks happen or not. Hold contingency centrally, release it against a named item in the RAID log, and return what is not needed at each gate.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md](../../playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md)

</details>

### 5. Adding people to a late software project is a reliable way to bring the date back.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Fred Brooks wrote in 1975 that adding people to a late software project makes it later. New people need time to learn and take time from those who know the system. Re-forecast, cut scope and remove waiting first.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md](../../playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md)

</details>

### 6. Likelihood and impact scores from 1 to 5 can be added up to size a project's contingency.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Scores sort the RAID log, but they cannot be added or compared with a budget. Size each top risk in money: its probability as a percentage times its impact. The sum of open money exposure is what contingency is held against.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/risks-raid-and-stage-gates.md](../../playbook/project-management/risks-raid-and-stage-gates.md)

</details>

### 7. At a stage gate, the decision should rest on the remaining cost and the remaining value of the project.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Money already spent cannot be recovered, so it is not a reason to continue. Ask: knowing what we know now, would we start this today? A stop supported by the evidence is a good result.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/risks-raid-and-stage-gates.md](../../playbook/project-management/risks-raid-and-stage-gates.md)

</details>

### 8. A status dimension whose key evidence is missing, such as a migration rehearsal that has not run, should be reported as amber at best.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Unknown is not green. An untested payment run, an unrun rehearsal or a supplier figure nobody has checked hides the risk until it is too late. Set colours by written rules that compare the forecast with the tolerance.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/status-reporting.md](../../playbook/project-management/status-reporting.md)

</details>

### 9. Percent complete of a task list is a reliable measure of project progress.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Tasks can be 90% complete for months, and the list hides scope growth. Report accepted increments, a burn-up chart with the scope line drawn, and a forecast range with a confidence level.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/status-reporting.md](../../playbook/project-management/status-reporting.md)

</details>

### 10. In earned value management, the schedule performance index drifts back towards 1.0 near the end of a project whether or not the project is late.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The schedule performance index (SPI) is measured in money, and earned value approaches the plan as work finishes. Use the cost performance index for cost and a throughput forecast for dates.

Read more: [playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md](../../playbook/project-management/planning-fixed-scope-and-budget.md)

</details>
